title: Instrumental Methods of Analysis
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L instrumental analysis curriculum: principles and instrumentation of UV-Vis and IR spectrophotometry, atomic absorption/emission spectroscopy, chromatographic methods (TLC, column, GC, HPLC), electroanalytical methods (potentiometry, conductometry, voltammetry/polarography), and basic mass spectrometry, with emphasis on Beer-Lambert law, instrument components, and method selection.

questions.question: The Beer-Lambert law relates absorbance (A) to concentration (c) and path length (b) as:
questions.correct_answer: A = εbc
questions.explanation: Absorbance is directly proportional to the molar absorptivity, path length, and concentration: A = εbc.

questions.question: In a UV-Vis spectrophotometer, the component that isolates a narrow band of wavelengths from the polychromatic source before it reaches the sample is the:
questions.correct_answer: Monochromator
questions.explanation: The monochromator (using a prism or diffraction grating) disperses light and selects a narrow wavelength band for analysis.

questions.question: A solution with molar absorptivity ε = 5000 dm3 mol-1 cm-1 gives an absorbance of 0.500 in a 1 cm cell. What is the concentration?
Deviations from Beer-Lambert linearity at high analyte concentrations are commonly attributed to:
options: Increased stray light and analyte-analyte interactions changing the effective absorptivity
Decreased path length of the cuvette
questions.correct_answer: Increased stray light and analyte-analyte interactions changing the effective absorptivity
questions.explanation: At high concentrations, deviations arise from chemical interactions between absorbing species and instrumental limitations such as stray light, causing the A-c plot to curve away from linearity.

questions.question: In infrared (IR) spectrophotometry, sample cells and windows are commonly made of materials such as NaCl or KBr because they:
options: Absorb strongly in the IR region
questions.correct_answer: Are transparent to infrared radiation
questions.explanation: Alkali halide salts like NaCl and KBr do not absorb in the mid-IR region, so they are used as windows/cell materials to allow IR radiation to pass through the sample.

questions.question: A strong, sharp absorption band around 1700 cm-1 in an IR spectrum is most characteristic of which functional group?
questions.correct_answer: C=O stretch (carbonyl)
questions.explanation: Carbonyl groups (aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters) show a strong, characteristic stretching absorption near 1650-1750 cm-1.

questions.question: In atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS), the hollow cathode lamp serves to:
options: Atomize the sample in a flame
Provide radiation of the exact wavelength absorbed by the element being determined
questions.correct_answer: Provide radiation of the exact wavelength absorbed by the element being determined
questions.explanation: The hollow cathode lamp is made of the element of interest and emits its characteristic line spectrum, matching the narrow absorption lines of ground-state atoms in the flame for selective, sensitive determination.

questions.question: In AAS, the sample is first converted into free gaseous ground-state atoms by a process called:
questions.correct_answer: Atomisation
questions.explanation: Atomisation (usually in a flame or graphite furnace) converts the sample into free ground-state atoms capable of absorbing radiation at their characteristic wavelength.

questions.question: Flame emission spectroscopy differs fundamentally from atomic absorption spectroscopy in that flame emission measures:
options: Light emitted by atoms that have been thermally excited and then return to the ground state
questions.correct_answer: Light emitted by atoms that have been thermally excited and then return to the ground state
questions.explanation: In flame emission spectroscopy, thermal energy from the flame excites atoms, which then emit characteristic radiation as they relax back to the ground state; AAS instead measures absorption by ground-state atoms.

questions.question: In thin layer chromatography (TLC), the retardation factor (Rf) is defined as:
options: Distance travelled by solvent front divided by distance travelled by the compound
Distance travelled by the compound divided by distance travelled by the solvent front
Time taken by the compound to elute
Mass of compound divided by mass of adsorbent
questions.correct_answer: Distance travelled by the compound divided by distance travelled by the solvent front
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front, a characteristic value used to identify compounds under given TLC conditions.

questions.question: In column chromatography, a compound that is more strongly adsorbed onto the stationary phase will generally:
options: Elute faster than weakly adsorbed compounds
Elute more slowly, requiring a larger elution volume
Not separate from the mobile phase at all
questions.correct_answer: Elute more slowly, requiring a larger elution volume
questions.explanation: Strongly adsorbed compounds spend more time associated with the stationary phase relative to the mobile phase, so they migrate down the column more slowly and elute later.

questions.question: In gas chromatography (GC), the mobile phase is:
options: An inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen
questions.correct_answer: An inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen
questions.explanation: GC uses an inert gas (e.g. He, N2, H2) as the mobile phase to carry vaporised analytes through the column; separation occurs based on interaction with the stationary phase and volatility.

questions.question: A key limitation of gas chromatography as an analytical technique is that it is generally only suitable for compounds that are:
options: Volatile and thermally stable, or can be derivatised to be so
questions.correct_answer: Volatile and thermally stable, or can be derivatised to be so
questions.explanation: GC requires the analyte to vaporise without decomposition as it passes through the heated column, restricting its direct use to volatile, thermally stable compounds.

questions.question: In high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), reverse-phase columns use a non-polar stationary phase (e.g. C18-bonded silica) with a relatively polar mobile phase; in this mode, the most polar analytes will:
options: Elute first, since they interact weakly with the non-polar stationary phase
questions.correct_answer: Elute first, since they interact weakly with the non-polar stationary phase
questions.explanation: In reverse-phase HPLC, polar solutes have weaker affinity for the non-polar stationary phase and are carried through faster by the polar mobile phase, eluting earlier than non-polar solutes.

questions.question: Which detector is most commonly paired with HPLC for compounds that absorb in the UV-visible region?
questions.correct_answer: UV-Vis (photodiode array) detector
questions.explanation: UV-Vis detectors are the most widely used HPLC detectors for analytes containing chromophores, measuring absorbance of the column effluent as it passes through a flow cell.

questions.question: The flame ionisation detector (FID) commonly used in GC responds primarily to:
options: Organic compounds containing carbon-hydrogen bonds, which produce ions when burned
questions.correct_answer: Organic compounds containing carbon-hydrogen bonds, which produce ions when burned
questions.explanation: FID burns eluting compounds in a hydrogen/air flame; organic compounds generate ions and electrons proportional to the number of C-H bonds, producing a measurable current.

questions.question: In potentiometry, the electrode whose potential is fixed and known, used as a comparison point, is the:
questions.correct_answer: Reference electrode
questions.explanation: The reference electrode (e.g. standard calomel or Ag/AgCl electrode) maintains a constant, known potential against which the indicator electrode's potential is measured.

questions.question: A glass electrode used to measure pH functions on the principle that:
options: It generates a potential proportional to the hydrogen ion activity across a thin glass membrane
It directly measures the colour of an indicator
It conducts a fixed current regardless of solution composition
It measures the boiling point of the solution
questions.correct_answer: It generates a potential proportional to the hydrogen ion activity across a thin glass membrane
questions.explanation: The glass electrode develops a membrane potential that varies with the difference in H+ activity between the internal reference solution and the test solution, following the Nernst equation.

questions.question: Conductometric titration is particularly useful for titrations where:
options: No suitable visual indicator exists or the solution is coloured/turbid
questions.correct_answer: No suitable visual indicator exists or the solution is coloured/turbid
questions.explanation: Conductometric titration follows changes in solution conductance as ions are consumed/produced, making it valuable when coloured or turbid solutions preclude visual indicators.

questions.question: In polarography, the dropping mercury electrode is used because it:
options: Provides a continuously renewed, reproducible electrode surface for each drop
Is completely inert and never participates in electrode reactions
Eliminates the need for a reference electrode
Cannot be used for reduction reactions
questions.correct_answer: Provides a continuously renewed, reproducible electrode surface for each drop
questions.explanation: Each falling mercury drop presents a fresh, reproducible surface, minimising fouling effects and giving reproducible current-voltage (polarographic) curves.

questions.question: In voltammetry, the diffusion current observed is directly proportional to the:
options: Concentration of the electroactive species in solution
questions.correct_answer: Concentration of the electroactive species in solution
questions.explanation: Under diffusion-controlled conditions, the limiting current is proportional to bulk analyte concentration, which is the basis of quantitative voltammetric analysis.

questions.question: In basic mass spectrometry, the molecular ion peak (M+) observed in the mass spectrum corresponds to:
options: A fragment with half the molecular mass
The intact molecule that has lost a single electron upon ionisation
questions.correct_answer: The intact molecule that has lost a single electron upon ionisation
questions.explanation: The molecular ion (M+) forms when the neutral molecule loses one electron during ionisation (e.g. electron impact), giving a peak at the molecular mass (minus the mass of an electron, which is negligible).

questions.question: The 'base peak' in a mass spectrum refers to the:
options: Peak with the lowest m/z value
Peak corresponding to the molecular ion only
Tallest (most intense) peak, arbitrarily assigned 100% relative abundance
questions.correct_answer: Tallest (most intense) peak, arbitrarily assigned 100% relative abundance
questions.explanation: The base peak is the most abundant ion observed and is set to 100% relative intensity, with all other peaks scaled against it.

questions.question: A calibration curve in quantitative instrumental analysis is constructed by:
options: Plotting instrument response against known concentrations of standards to determine unknown concentrations by interpolation
Measuring the unknown sample only, without standards
Recording the boiling point of the analyte
questions.correct_answer: Plotting instrument response against known concentrations of standards to determine unknown concentrations by interpolation
questions.explanation: A series of standards of known concentration is measured to establish a response-concentration relationship, which is then used to interpolate the concentration of an unknown from its measured response.

questions.question: The limit of detection (LOD) of an instrumental method is best described as the:
options: Highest concentration the instrument can measure
Lowest concentration of analyte that can be reliably distinguished from the blank/background noise
Concentration at which the calibration curve becomes non-linear
questions.correct_answer: Lowest concentration of analyte that can be reliably distinguished from the blank/background noise
questions.explanation: LOD is the smallest analyte concentration that produces a signal statistically distinguishable from the blank, commonly taken as three times the standard deviation of the blank signal divided by the calibration slope.

questions.question: The method of standard addition is particularly useful in instrumental analysis when:
options: The sample matrix significantly affects the instrument response (matrix effects)
The analyte is present in extremely high concentration
questions.correct_answer: The sample matrix significantly affects the instrument response (matrix effects)
questions.explanation: Standard addition adds known amounts of analyte directly to aliquots of the sample itself, compensating for matrix effects that would distort a calibration curve made from pure standards.

questions.question: In choosing between UV-Vis spectrophotometry and AAS for determining trace metal ions in a water sample, AAS is generally preferred because it offers:
options: Lower cost with no instrumentation required
Greater selectivity and sensitivity for individual metal elements
The ability to identify organic functional groups
Faster results with no sample preparation needed
questions.correct_answer: Greater selectivity and sensitivity for individual metal elements
questions.explanation: AAS exploits characteristic atomic absorption lines specific to each element, giving high selectivity and low detection limits for trace metals compared to general UV-Vis methods.

questions.question: A chromophore, in the context of UV-Vis spectroscopy, is:
options: A part of a molecule responsible for its colour/light absorption, typically containing conjugated pi-electron systems
The solvent used to dissolve the sample
The detector component of the spectrophotometer
questions.correct_answer: A part of a molecule responsible for its colour/light absorption, typically containing conjugated pi-electron systems
questions.explanation: Chromophores such as C=C, C=O, and aromatic rings undergo electronic transitions (e.g. pi to pi*) that absorb UV-visible light, giving rise to the observed spectrum.

questions.question: Before running a sample on an AAS instrument for lead determination, an analyst prepares a blank and three standard solutions. The main purpose of the blank is to:
options: Correct for background absorbance/signal not due to the analyte
Increase the sensitivity of the flame
Replace the need for a hollow cathode lamp
questions.correct_answer: Correct for background absorbance/signal not due to the analyte
questions.explanation: The blank (containing no analyte) accounts for solvent, matrix, and instrumental background signals, which are subtracted from sample readings to isolate the true analyte signal.

questions.question: In ion-exchange chromatography, separation of charged species is achieved primarily through:
options: Differences in affinity of ions for oppositely charged sites on the stationary phase resin
questions.correct_answer: Differences in affinity of ions for oppositely charged sites on the stationary phase resin
questions.explanation: Ion-exchange resins carry fixed charged functional groups that reversibly bind oppositely charged analyte ions with varying affinity, enabling their separation as the mobile phase elutes them differentially.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical component of a single-beam UV-Vis spectrophotometer?
questions.correct_answer: Column packed with stationary phase
questions.explanation: A packed column is a chromatography component, not part of a spectrophotometer, which instead comprises a source, monochromator, sample compartment, and detector.

questions.question: In IR spectroscopy, a sample is often prepared as a KBr pellet for solid samples mainly because KBr:
options: Is highly coloured, enhancing the spectrum
Is IR-transparent and can be pressed with the solid sample into a clear disc
Reacts chemically with the analyte to improve detection
Is a strong absorbent of infrared radiation
questions.correct_answer: Is IR-transparent and can be pressed with the solid sample into a clear disc
questions.explanation: KBr does not absorb in the mid-IR region and, being pliable under pressure, forms a transparent disc when mixed and pressed with a solid sample, allowing IR light to pass through for analysis.

questions.question: Precision in an instrumental method refers to:
options: How close a measured value is to the true value
The reproducibility of repeated measurements under the same conditions
The range over which the instrument can operate
questions.correct_answer: The reproducibility of repeated measurements under the same conditions
questions.explanation: Precision describes the closeness of agreement among repeated measurements of the same sample, distinct from accuracy, which describes closeness to the true value.
